claims.text: High-temperature oxidizing exposure causes diffusion-mediated segregation of Mg from the metastable solid solution.
Mg segregation promotes nucleation and growth of nanoscale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates disrupt formation of a uniform protective oxide scale.
Disruption of the protective oxide scale reduces corrosion resistance.
Disruption of the protective oxide scale reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Lower oxygen activity or shorter exposure times hinder intermetallic precipitation.
Suppressing intermetallic precipitation retains the metastable solid-solution state.
Retention of the metastable solid solution produces a more coherent and protective oxide film.
The relevant precipitates form preferentially at grain boundaries or other high-diffusivity sites.
Temperature-accelerated Mg diffusion produces local supersaturation and precipitation of intermetallic compounds.
A continuous, stable oxide film is necessary for effective corrosion and oxidation protection.
Air-aged samples will contain more Mg-rich intermetallic phases than the initial metastable alloy.
Air-aged samples will develop a discontinuous, less protective oxide scale relative to the initial state.
Air aging will degrade corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable alloy.
Inert-aged samples will largely retain the homogenized solid-solution state.
Inert-aged samples will develop a more uniform and adherent oxide layer and preserve better protective properties.
Diffusion-controlled transformation becomes significant above approximately 600 °C when exposure duration is sufficient.
Below the stated service-regime thresholds, the metastable state persists without significant precipitation.

contradictions.description: The inert treatment is defined as minimizing oxidation, yet the inert-aged sample is predicted to develop a uniform, adherent oxide layer during that treatment. No subsequent oxidizing exposure is specified to generate or evaluate that layer.
